analysis.one_liner: Overhauls credit reporting: easier error disputes, free credit scores and freezes, and shorter reporting of bad debts.
analysis.headline: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill with 8 Democratic cosponsors in May 2016; it died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Credit Reporting Act to make it easier to fix errors on credit reports, add a free appeal when a dispute goes against you, and let courts order credit bureaus to stop unlawful practices. It would ban most employers from using credit checks in hiring, remove bad marks faster — including paid medical debt, rehabbed private student loans, and debts caused by predatory lenders or financial abusers — and give consumers free credit scores alongside their free annual reports. It would also ban auto-renewing "free trial" credit monitoring subscriptions, cap fees on credit products, require free credit freezes for identity theft victims, and push the bureaus to serve customers in 10 languages and accessible formats.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose reports contain errors — one FTC study cited in the bill's findings found 26% of people had at least one potentially material error — along with job applicants with damaged credit, patients with paid-off medical bills, private student loan borrowers who rebuild their payments, victims of predatory mortgage lending and for-profit college fraud, survivors of domestic financial abuse, and identity theft victims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with credit report errors and damaged credit

how_it_helps.text: Creates a free right to appeal when a credit bureau's investigation of a dispute comes out against the consumer, and requires bureaus to actually review documents consumers submit rather than rubber-stamping the data furnisher's answer [S2].
Bans the use of credit reports for most employment decisions, ending what the bill's findings call a "catch-22" in which job loss damages credit and damaged credit then blocks getting hired [S2][S3].

Removes adverse information faster: shortens how long most negative items stay on reports, requires expedited removal of fully paid or settled medical debt, erases delinquency records for private student loan borrowers who make 9 on-time payments over 10 months, and restores credit for predatory lending victims, defrauded for-profit college students, and survivors of financial abuse [S2].

Gives consumers free credit scores with their free annual reports, requires bureaus to disclose prominently how the scores they sell differ from the ones lenders actually use, and requires lenders to show borrowers the reports and scores used before they sign for a car, mortgage, or private student loan [S2].
Bans automatic renewal of "free trial" credit monitoring and credit score products, bans deceptive marketing of them, and lets the CFPB cap what bureaus charge consumers for these products [S2].

Requires free credit freezes for consumers who suspect identity theft, free credit monitoring and identity protection for those who qualify, removal of fraud-related inquiries from reports, and multilingual, disability-accessible customer service from bureaus and furnishers [S2].
Lets courts award injunctive relief against companies that willfully or negligently violate the law, so a consumer can force an unlawful practice to stop rather than only collect damages [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The three nationwide credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) and sellers of credit monitoring and score products, who would face accuracy mandates, a free appeal right, fee caps, and bans on auto-renewing subscription products. Creditors, debt collectors, and other data furnishers would bear new record-keeping and notice costs. Employers would lose the ability to screen job applicants by credit history, and private student lenders would lose the credit-report leverage of permanent default records.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, credit-monitoring sellers, and debt collectors

drawbacks.text: Creditors and other data furnishers would have to keep records backing every reported item for as long as it can appear on a report, and send advance warnings before reporting negative information — real compliance costs that could be passed along in credit prices [S2].

Banning credit checks for employment removes a screening tool some employers say helps them reduce theft and liability for sensitive positions, even though a study cited in the bill's findings found credit history does not actually predict job performance or turnover [S3].

Requiring staffed, independent investigations (with US-based dispute staff), 10-language customer service, and accessibility formats would force the bureaus to replace their low-cost, quota-driven dispute systems with more expensive ones [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits run to roughly 200 million adults whose files sit in three companies' databases and who, by law, cannot opt out: easier and fairer error fixes, faster erasure of paid and unfairly-reported debts, free access to the scores lenders actually use, and protection from identity theft and predatory subscription sales. The main costs are compliance expenses for the bureaus, furnishers, and employers — costs the bill's findings argue fall on companies that already profit from an involuntary data relationship and currently run disputes through five-minute quota calls. The burden is one-sided toward the industry, and the strongest good-faith objection is the employment credit check ban, which is a real tradeoff for some employers but is aimed at a practice the record shows does not predict job performance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the Comprehensive Consumer Credit Reporting Reform Act on May 19, 2016 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the complete action history shows no action after the referral, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].
The bill drew 8 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus and credit-monitoring sellers avoided the accuracy mandates, free appeal right, fee caps, and product bans, and employers kept the ability to screen job applicants by credit history.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its findings documenting credit report errors, quota-driven dispute handling, and industry marketing practices.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after its referral to his committee; the bill saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Consumer data industry (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
against.what_they_did: The bill's findings accuse the bureaus of quota-driven, rubber-stamp dispute handling and of luring consumers into auto-renewing monitoring subscriptions, and the industry faced losing revenue from fee-capped products, free scores, and mandatory free credit freezes; no formal opposition is recorded in the congressional record because the bill never received a hearing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never moved in the Republican-chaired Financial Services Committee [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill imposes accuracy and independent-investigation duties, a free dispute appeal, disclosure of public record sources, free scores with annual reports, free credit freezes for fraud victims, fee caps on direct-to-consumer products, and a ban on auto-renewing trial subscriptions — a direct hit to both their reporting operations and their consumer-products revenue. These companies hold files on about 200 million adults who cannot take their business elsewhere.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and credit score sellers
industries.note: Bans automatic renewal of promotional-trial products, bans deceptive marketing, requires prominent disclosure that the scores sold to consumers differ from those lenders use, and lets the CFPB cap prices — targeting a market in which consumers spent about $3.5 billion in 2010 on identity protection products.

Requires expedited removal of fully paid or settled medical debt and shortens how long most adverse information stays on reports, shrinking the leverage collection tradelines give them over consumers; the CFPB found half of all collection tradelines are medical bills.

industries.industry: Employers that use credit checks in hiring
industries.note: Bans credit checks for most employment decisions, removing a screening tool these employers used on up to 60% of hires; the bill's findings argue the practice disproportionately screens out minority and unemployed applicants.

Must erase delinquency and default records for borrowers who make 9 on-time payments over 10 months, and remove records tied to defrauded for-profit college attendance, and must show borrowers their reports before signing — cutting the credit-report consequences that make private loans risky to default on.

Face new record-retention, advance negative-information notices, and independent investigation duties, but also benefit from a reporting system the bill's findings say is riddled with errors that undermine accurate underwriting.
